paragraphs: This checklist is only for self-questioning and does not constitute hiring criteria, an ability score or a safety assessment. This page follows US O*NET-SOC 41-1012.00, First-Line Supervisors of Non-Retail Sales Workers (the fixed index assigns this asset the corresponding Chinese title; the body follows the official occupational scope). First-line non-retail sales management roles vary greatly: wholesale and distribution; industrial, equipment and building materials sales; insurance and financial services sales; advertising and media sales; enterprise services and solutions; pharmaceutical and specialized product agencies; call-based and inside sales teams; and leasing and rental agreement business. A role may lead one product line or region, or manage multiple salespeople, channel partners and outside agents. Before comparing roles or career paths, check education and experience requirements; required industry qualifications or licenses, such as insurance, securities or credit; travel, customer visit and assessment-pressure demands; performance assessment and commission structures, including base pay, commissions, bonuses and quotas; and responsibility for budgets, pricing, inventory and personnel management.

Test your fit with a paper-based exercise. Given an entirely fictional sales team assignment covering a product line or territory, target customers and quotas; current-period sales revenue, new customer and payment collection targets; available personnel, channels and support resources; products, inventory, delivery and pricing policies; a customer complaint, performance shortfall or pricing and delivery conflict; and required scheduling, assignments, process coaching, performance review and reporting, write a weekly meeting plan and target breakdown, customer visit and follow-up cadence, quote, discount and pricing policy boundaries, performance discussions and improvement plans, complaint handling and cross-department coordination paths, and records and reports related to sales, inventory and payment collection. Identify decisions that must be made by sales, finance or legal managers.

Signals worth considering: willingness to lead a sales team long term and bear quota and performance pressure; ability to improve the team through process management and coaching; and willingness to handle customer complaints and cross-department coordination. Signals calling for caution: reluctance to face repeated performance assessments, rejection and conflict; difficulty accepting travel and customer visit rhythms; or imagining that the work requires only personal selling without leading people and managing processes.
This card is a career exploration reference, not a hiring, ability-scoring, performance or compliance conclusion.

First decide whether you want to make non-retail sales management a long-term career. It requires leading sales teams over time; bearing quota, payment collection and customer relationship targets; organizing process management under company policies and industry standards; and assuming management responsibility for team conduct and customer commitments. Test this through the paper-based exercise and seven-day tasks on this page.

The work of First-Line Supervisors of Non-Retail Sales Workers follows a cycle of target breakdown, scheduling and assignments; process management, customer visits and sales support; performance review, coaching and improvement; quotes, discounts, pricing policies and inventory; sales, inventory and payment collection records and reports; and recruiting, training and cross-department coordination. At the start of a period, break down sales revenue, new customer and collection targets by person and timeframe, prepare schedules and assign specific duties. Monitor sales staff performance to ensure goals are met, assist with difficult or complex duties, and direct and supervise employees engaged in sales, inventory counts, checking cash receipts or providing specific services. Review quotes, discounts and payment terms for compliance with pricing policies and profitability requirements; participate in establishing merchandise pricing policies based on profitability; count inventory and replenish at specified levels; inspect products purchased for resale or received for storage for condition; and inspect merchandise for correct pricing and display and performance as advertised. Listen to and resolve customer complaints about services, products or personnel, and communicate with management as needed to develop methods and procedures to increase sales, expand markets and promote business. Maintain purchasing, sales and requisition records and prepare sales and inventory reports for management and budget departments. Budgeting, accounting and personnel duties may accompany supervision. Participate in recruiting, training and evaluating personnel; analyze sales territories for growth potential and set quotas; coordinate promotions such as displays and advertising copy; and prepare leasing or rental agreements specifying charges and payment procedures. Visit retailers and sales representatives to promote products and gather information, and attend company meetings to exchange product information and coordinate with other departments. Priorities vary substantially by setting: wholesale and distribution emphasize channels, inventory and collections; industrial, equipment and building materials sales emphasize solutions, follow-up cycles and bidding support; insurance and finance emphasize compliance, suitability, licensing and retention; advertising and media emphasize proposals, campaign placement and payment terms; enterprise services and solutions emphasize needs discovery, multiple decision-makers and contracts; pharmaceuticals and specialized products emphasize compliant visits, access and scientific communication; call-based and inside sales emphasize lead conversion, script quality and volume; and leasing and rental agreements emphasize terms, equipment condition and renewals.

US O*NET-SOC 41-1012.00, First-Line Supervisors of Non-Retail Sales Workers: directly supervise and coordinate the activities of sales workers other than retail sales workers; may perform budgeting, accounting and personnel duties in addition to supervision.

Work context | These supervisors primarily break down targets, manage processes and review performance. Workload is driven by quarterly and monthly targets, customer decision cycles and promotional rhythms. O*NET work context data show mainly regular schedules (regular, 50%), with irregular schedules at 39% and seasonal schedules at 11%. For weekly hours, 88% work more than 40 hours and 12% work 40 hours. Contact with others is constant for 73% and most of the time for 25%. Daily face-to-face discussions are reported by 91%; daily telephone conversations, 97%; and daily email, 100%. Teamwork is extremely important to 68% and very important to 30%; coordinating or leading others is extremely important to 61% and very important to 35%. Extremely exact or highly accurate work is required by a combined 78% (extremely important, 45%; very important, 33%; important, 21%). Consequences of error are extremely serious for 11%, serious for 26%, fairly serious for 28% and not serious at all for 35%. Strict deadlines occur daily for 69% and once a week or more for 26%. Conflict situations occur daily for 15%, once a week or more for 34%, once a month or more for 38% and once a year or more for 13%. Dealing with unpleasant, angry or discourteous people occurs daily for 14%, once a week or more for 23%, once a month or more for 36% and never for 11%. Standing is mainly less than half the time (54%), with never at 11%. Walking or running less than half the time is reported by 44% and never by 23%. Sitting continually or almost continually is reported by 37% and more than half the time by 22%. Working indoors in controlled environments occurs daily for 85%. Outdoor exposure to all weather occurs daily for 26% and never for 28%; contaminants daily for 17% and never for 64%; hazardous equipment never for 81%; and distracting noise daily for 29% and never for 27%. Work is highly automated for 13%, moderately for 16%, slightly for 38% and not at all for 32%. Responsibility for others' health and safety is very high for 29%, high for 26%, moderate for 22% and limited for 17%. Decisions are made daily by 65% and once a week or more by 28%. Decisions affect very important outcomes for 65% and important outcomes for 30%. Decision-making freedom is considerable for 29%, some for 58% and very little for 11%. Freedom to determine tasks, priorities and goals is considerable for 54%, some for 34% and none for 11%. Competition is extremely intense for 31% and moderately intense for 48%. Dealing with external customers or the public is extremely important to 62% and important to 21%.

Sales occupations are often confused. Distinguish them by responsibilities and outputs. This occupation is a first-line non-retail sales management role primarily producing team target breakdown, process management, performance review, and customer and pricing policy management. Wholesale and manufacturing sales representatives, service sales representatives and advertising sales representatives develop customers, close sales and collect payments. Insurance sales representatives and securities, commodities and financial services sales agents provide licensed sales and suitability services. Sales managers handle multiteam, product-line and regional strategies and budgets with a broader management span. Customer service representatives handle inquiries, answers and service tickets, usually without sales targets. First-line supervisors of retail sales workers manage store retail operations, displays, checkout and customer service in retail settings. This occupation excludes roles primarily focused on retail store operations or sales management positions primarily focused on strategy and budgets.

subject.name: First-Line Supervisors of Non-Retail Sales Workers
subject.summary: Directly supervise and coordinate the activities of sales workers other than retail sales workers; may perform budgeting, accounting and personnel duties in addition to supervision. Tasks include monitoring sales staff performance to ensure goals are met; assisting employees with difficult or complex duties; directing and supervising employees engaged in sales, inventory counts, checking cash receipts or providing specific services; listening to and resolving customer complaints about services, products or personnel; keeping purchasing, sales and requisition records; recruiting, training and evaluating personnel; communicating with company management to develop methods and procedures to increase sales, expand markets and promote business; preparing work schedules and assigning specific duties; attending company meetings to exchange product information and coordinate with other departments; visiting retailers and sales representatives to promote products and gather information; establishing merchandise pricing policies based on profitability requirements; preparing sales and inventory reports for management and budget departments; inspecting products purchased for resale or received for storage to determine condition; inspecting merchandise to ensure correct pricing and display and performance as advertised; analyzing sales territory details to assess growth potential and set quotas; counting inventory and replenishing stock at specified levels; coordinating promotions such as merchandise displays and advertising copy; and preparing leasing or rental agreements specifying charges and payment procedures for machinery, tools or other items.
